source: Windsor, P.A. 2014. 'FAQ's on FMD Essentials for Field Staff' -- ACIAR/USYD Mekong Livestock Research project resource (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com)
text: This FAQ sheet for field/extension staff summarises FMD essentials in a quick-reference format. Cause: a virus with 7 types and many strains, with O and A types most common in South-East Asia; it infects cattle, buffalo, and pigs (not humans) and spreads between all three. Spread: FMD is described as the most rapidly spreading animal disease in the world -- via direct animal-to-animal contact, contaminated mud/dirt/grass, human clothing/shoes/vehicles, or feeding infected meat scraps/milk to pigs; even healthy-looking animals may already be incubating and spreading it. Prevention: never buy animals from a place of unknown FMD status, and isolate any new animal for 2 weeks even from a 'clean' source; vaccinate with affordable ($1/dose), effective multivalent vaccines (since O-only vaccine will not protect against A-type infection) that give about 6 months' protection. Treatment: isolate infected animals in a clean area, provide water, soft feed (not rice straw), and rest; treat sores topically with disinfectants (e.g. methylene blue) and astringents (vinegar, lemon juice); antibiotics are costly and unnecessary against the virus itself. After recovery, most animals are immune to that specific strain for at least 18 months, so keeping recovered animals is usually preferable to replacing them. Five community-level control priorities are given: separate infected/uninfected animals within the household; keep infected animals and their handlers out of shared grazing areas at village level; strictly restrict animal movement and never sell sick animals; clean shoes/clothing/vehicles when moving between places; and maintain routine vaccination. The sheet stresses FMD must be distinguished from Haemorrhagic Septicaemia (HS), since HS often needs antibiotic treatment while FMD does not.
